lede: Everything in Topic 10, split into two bands. sections.title: Charge and current: what is actually moving

parts.title: The atom, and what moves
parts.html:
ParticleWhereRelative massRelative charge
Protonnucleus1+1
Neutronnucleus10
Electronshells around the nucleusvery small (about 1/2000)−1

An atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so it is neutral. In a metal, the outer electrons are not tied to one atom: they are free electrons that can drift through the lattice of positive ions. That drift is an electric current.

Electric current is the rate of flow of charge: how many coulombs pass a point each second. $I = Q \div t$; one ampere is one coulomb per second. In metals the moving charges are electrons; in a solution they can be ions. Electrons carry negative charge, so they move from the negative terminal to the positive; conventional current is drawn the other way, from + to −, and every diagram and rule in this topic uses conventional current.

The electrons do not travel fast — about a millimetre a second — but they all start moving at once when the switch closes, so the lamp lights at once.

sections.title: Circuit diagrams, symbols and meters

parts.title: The symbols
parts.html: Draw circuits with a ruler: straight wires, right-angled corners, no gaps, symbols on the wire (not floating beside it). A cell is one; a battery is two or more cells joined. The long thin line is the positive terminal. Conventional current leaves it and goes round to the short thick line.

parts.title: The two meters
parts.html:
An ammeter measures current in amps (A). It goes in series with the component, so the same current that goes through the component goes through the meter. A voltmeter measures the potential difference in volts (V) across a component, so it goes in parallel with it — one lead each side.

The June 2023 report (Q2(a)): the voltmeter was "often across the variable resistor or the battery" instead of the component asked for, and "a voltmeter is never connected in series". The June 2024 scheme (Q8(a), 3 marks): variable resistor in series, ammeter in series with the lamp, voltmeter in parallel with the lamp — one mark each. The June 2025 report (Q10(c)): "a misplaced voltmeter" kept answers at Level 1.

The voltmeter drawn as a separate branch with one lead on each side of the resistor only — not across the cell, not across the ammeter.
Correct symbols: circle-A and circle-V, rectangle for the resistor, long-and-short lines for the cell, a gap with a hinged line for the switch.

sections.title: Charge, current and time: Q = I × t

parts.title: The equation and the two rules
parts.html:
$Q = I \times t$: charge (C) = current (A) × time (s). A 2 A current for 1 minute moves $2 \times 60 = 120$ C. Two conversions catch people out: minutes to seconds, and mA to A (divide by 1000). The June 2025 report (Q4(c)): many "made no attempt at conversion from mA to A" and lost the evaluation mark; the same in Q10(a)(i). Write $2.5$ mA $= 0.0025$ A before you substitute.

Closed circuit (10.10): a current needs a complete loop of conductors and a source of potential difference (cell, battery, supply). Open the switch and the loop is broken — the current is zero everywhere in that loop at once.

Conservation of current (10.11): charge cannot pile up or vanish at a junction, so the total current into a junction equals the total current out. 0.5 A into a junction that splits two ways with 0.2 A in one branch means 0.3 A in the other. The June 2024 scheme (Q2(a)) tested exactly this: the currents in the branches must add up to the current from the battery.

Units: C — 250 mA = 0.25 A and 4 min = 240 s before substituting

sections.title: Potential difference: energy per coulomb, and E = Q × V

parts.title: What a volt is
parts.html:
Potential difference (pd, also called voltage) across a component is the energy transferred per unit charge passing through it: $V = E \div Q$. So the volt is a joule per coulomb: across a 6 V lamp, every coulomb that passes transfers 6 J of energy (to light and heat). Rearranged, $E = Q \times V$: energy transferred (J) = charge moved (C) × pd (V).

Across the source, the pd is the energy given to each coulomb (from the chemical store of the cell); across a component, it is the energy taken from each coulomb. Round a series circuit, the energy given per coulomb equals the energy taken per coulomb in total — the pds across the components add up to the pd of the source (N6).

The June 2024 scheme (Q8(d), 2 marks): "potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge passed" (1), "so the units of pd are J/C" (1). Say both halves.

With $Q = I \times t$, $E = I \times t \times V$ — the same as 10.27's $E = I \times V \times t$ (N10).

sections.title: Resistance and V = I × R

parts.title: Resistance
parts.html:
$V = I \times R$: pd (V) = current (A) × resistance (Ω). Resistance is the ratio of pd to current, $R = V \div I$ — the number of volts needed to drive one amp. A 1 Ω component passes 1 A with 1 V across it; a 100 Ω one needs 100 V for the same current.

Changing resistance changes current (10.12): for a fixed pd, more resistance → less current, in inverse proportion (double R, halve I). A variable resistor is a long coil of resistance wire with a sliding contact: moving the slider puts more or less wire in the circuit, changing the resistance and so the current — which is how a dimmer, a volume control and the core practical work. The June 2023 report (Q2(b)(iv)): the variable resistor reduces the current by increasing the resistance of the circuit; "slowing down the current" and "decreasing the resistance" were rejected, and many confused it with a thermistor.

Units trap: kΩ × 1000 to Ω, mA ÷ 1000 to A. $6$ V across $2$ kΩ gives $I = 6 \div 2000 = 0.003$ A $= 3$ mA.

parts.title: Resistance from V and I
parts.question: A pd of 6.0 V across a resistor gives a current of 9.1 mA. Calculate the resistance.
steps: $R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{6.0}{0.0091} = 660$ Ω (3 s.f.) — the June 2024 scheme's own numbers (Q2(b)(iii)).

  • …and for the same pd a larger resistance gives a smaller current ($I = V/R$).

questions.text: The resistance in a circuit is doubled while the pd stays the same. The current…

sections.title: Series and parallel circuits: the rules
equations: \text{series: } I \text{ same},\ V_1 + V_2 = V,\ R = R_1 + R_2
\text{parallel: } V \text{ same},\ I_1 + I_2 = I,\ R < \text{smallest}

parts.title: The rules
parts.html:
SeriesParallel
Currentthe same at every point (one path)splits at the junction: the branch currents add up to the supply current
Potential differenceshared between the components: their pds add up to the supply pd — the bigger resistance takes the bigger sharethe same across every branch (each branch is connected straight across the supply)
Resistanceadds: $R = R_1 + R_2$ — more than any oneless than the smallest branch resistance
Switch / breakone switch controls everything; one broken component stops alleach branch can have its own switch; a broken branch leaves the others working

Why series increases resistance: the current has to pass through both resistors one after the other — more wire to push through — so the same pd drives less current: higher total resistance.

Why parallel decreases resistance: adding a branch gives the current another path; the same pd drives current through both branches at once, so the total current increases while the pd is unchanged — a smaller total resistance ($R = V/I$). The June 2024 scheme (Q2(b)(iv), 3 marks, for a resistor removed from parallel): total resistance increases (1) because the current decreases (1) while the voltage stays the same (1); "fewer paths for the current" accepted.

Edexcel asks you to calculate in series circuits (10.15) and to explain parallel ones (10.14): you are not expected to use the $1/R$ formula. The June 2025 report (Q10(c)): Level 1 answers "confused resistance and voltage" — keep the three quantities separate.

parts.title: A series calculation
parts.question: A 6 V battery is connected in series with a 10 Ω resistor and a 20 Ω resistor. Calculate (a) the total resistance, (b) the current, (c) the pd across each resistor.
steps: (b) $I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{6}{30} = 0.2$ A — the same current through both.
(c) $V_{10} = I \times R = 0.2 \times 10 = 2$ V; $V_{20} = 0.2 \times 20 = 4$ V. Check: $2 + 4 = 6$ V, the battery's pd. The larger resistor takes the larger share.

sections.title: I–V characteristics: resistor, filament lamp, diode

parts.title: The three shapes
parts.html: An I–V graph plots the current through a component (y) against the pd across it (x), for both directions of current (negative values on both axes). The resistance at any point is $R = V \div I$ using the values at that point.

graph.alt: Fixed resistor: a straight line through the origin — current proportional to pd, resistance constant (10 Ω here).

parts.title: Filament lamp
parts.html: The lamp's graph is a curve that gets less steep as the pd increases: each extra volt gives less extra current, so the resistance increases with pd. The filament is getting hotter (T3 explains why that raises the resistance). The June 2024 scheme (Q8(b)(ii)): "as potential difference increases current increases" (1) and "non-linear — curve, changing gradient" (1); Q8(b)(iii): resistance from $R = V/I$ at two points showing it increasing, or "the gradient decreases as pd increases" for 2 marks.

graph.alt: Filament lamp: a curve that flattens as pd increases — the resistance increases as the filament gets hotter.

parts.title: Diode
parts.html: A diode conducts in one direction only: for negative pd the current is zero (very high resistance); for positive pd nothing happens until about 0.7 V, then the current rises steeply (low resistance). The June 2025 report (Q6(b)): the mark was for "diodes allow current in one direction only"; "it limits the current" and "it is an LED indicator" scored nothing.

graph.alt: Diode: no current for negative pd (very high resistance); for positive pd above about 0.7 V the current rises steeply (low resistance).

parts.title: Reading a resistance

sections.title: LDRs and thermistors

parts.title: Light-dependent resistor
parts.html: An LDR (light-dependent resistor) has a resistance that decreases as the light intensity increases: very high in the dark, low in bright light (the graph is for one particular LDR). Uses: street lights and garden lights that come on at dusk, automatic brightness on a phone screen, burglar alarms triggered by a shadow.

graph.alt: LDR: the resistance falls as the light intensity rises.

parts.title: Thermistor
parts.html:
A thermistor has a resistance that decreases as the temperature increases (the spec covers negative temperature coefficient thermistors only). Uses: thermostats in ovens, fridges and central heating; car engine-temperature sensors; fire alarms; a digital thermometer. The June 2023 report: many students described a variable resistor as if it were a thermistor — a variable resistor is changed by hand; a thermistor changes by itself with temperature.

How the circuits that use them work — the pd sharing — is in T5.

graph.alt: Thermistor (NTC): the resistance falls as the temperature rises.

parts.question: Describe how the resistance of a thermistor changes with temperature, using the graph above. (2 marks)
steps: As the temperature increases the resistance decreases (from 10 kΩ at 0 °C to under 1 kΩ at 100 °C).
The change is not linear: the resistance falls steeply at first and then more slowly — the curve flattens.

sections.title: The heating effect of a current

parts.title: Why resistors get hot
parts.html:
When there is a current in a resistor there is an energy transfer that heats the resistor (10.22). Why (10.24): the free electrons collide with the ions in the metal's lattice as they are pushed through; each collision transfers energy to the ion, which vibrates more — and more vibration is a higher temperature. The electrical work done against the resistance is dissipated as thermal energy to the surroundings (10.23). That is also why a hot filament has a higher resistance: the ions vibrate more, so the electrons collide more often (T3).

Reducing the waste (10.25): energy transferred to heat in a wire is $I^2R$ per second, so use wires with low resistance — thick (large cross-section), short, made of a good conductor (copper). The June 2025 report (Q3(d)): the better cable has the thicker copper wire — lower resistance, so it carries a higher current safely with less heating; "thicker insulation stops energy loss" is wrong, and "bigger" alone scored nothing: say what is bigger and why it matters.

Heating effect wantedHeating effect unwanted
electric heaters, kettles, toasters, ovens, hair dryers; filament lamps (the filament glows); fuses (the wire melts when the current is too large)wires and cables warming (wasted energy, lower efficiency); electronics overheating; fire risk if a cable carries too much current

parts.question: Explain why a resistor gets hot when there is a current in it. (3 marks)
steps: The current is a flow of electrons through the metal; they collide with the ions in the lattice.
Each collision transfers energy to the ions, making them vibrate more — the resistor's temperature rises.
The energy is transferred from the electrical pathway to the thermal store of the resistor and then dissipated to the surroundings.

sections.title: Power and energy: the four equations

parts.title: Choosing the equation
parts.html:
Power is the energy transferred per second: $P = E \div t$, in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). A 2 kW kettle transfers 2000 J every second. A device's power rating (on its label) tells you how quickly it transfers energy from the mains or a battery: energy transferred $= P \times t$ (10.42) — the higher the rating and the longer it runs, the more the energy store of the supply falls.

You knowUse
current and pd$P = I \times V$ (10.30: the power transferred by any device is its current × the pd across it)
current and resistance$P = I^2 \times R$ (a resistor's heating)
energy and time$P = E \div t$
current, pd and time$E = I \times V \times t$
power rating and time$E = P \times t$ — seconds, for joules

Why $P = IV$: each coulomb transfers $V$ joules, and $I$ coulombs pass each second, so $I \times V$ joules per second. Why $P = I^2R$: substitute $V = IR$. The June 2025 report (Q3(b)): a straightforward $P = IV$ lost marks to calculator slips — "250 ÷ 0.53" instead of ×; write the substitution before pressing anything.

Time in seconds unless the question works in hours; the June 2023 report (Q8(b)(i)) — the commonest error in an $E = IVt$ charging-time question was not converting MJ to J and hours to seconds, and a comparison only scored if the unit of the calculated time was stated.

steps: (a) $P = I \times V$, so $I = \dfrac{P}{V} = \dfrac{2300}{230} = 10$ A.
(b) $E = P \times t = 2300 \times 180 = 414\,000$ J $= 414$ kJ (or $E = IVt = 10 \times 230 \times 180$, the same).

sections.title: Mains electricity: a.c., the three wires, fuses and earthing

parts.title: d.c. and a.c.
parts.html: Direct current (d.c.) is movement of charge in one direction only; cells and batteries supply d.c. Alternating current (a.c.) is movement of charge that changes direction repeatedly — the pd swings positive and negative. The UK mains is a.c. at a frequency of 50 Hz (50 cycles a second) and a pd of about 230 V. In the home, energy is transferred from the a.c. mains or from batteries to motors (kinetic) and heating devices (thermal) (10.32).

parts.title: The three wires and the safety parts
parts.html:
WireColourpdJob
Livebrown230 V (alternating)carries the current to the appliance from the supply; the dangerous one
Neutralblue0 Vcompletes the circuit — carries the current back to the supply
Earthgreen and yellow0 Va safety wire connected to the metal case; carries no current unless there is a fault

Fuse: a thin wire in the live wire, rated at a current a little above the appliance's normal current (3 A, 5 A, 13 A). If the current exceeds the rating, the fuse wire heats up and melts, which breaks the circuit and cuts off the current. Say melts: a fuse does not explode, and "blows" is not the physics. The June 2025 scheme (Q3(c)(ii)) gave two marks for "the fuse wire melts" and "this breaks the circuit"; answers that did not say what the fuse does scored one.

Circuit breaker: an automatic switch (an electromagnet) that trips when the current is too large; it does the fuse's job but faster, and it can be reset instead of replaced. The 2025 scheme accepted circuit breaker, earth wire, cable clamp, socket covers and insulation as safety devices "other than a fuse".

Earth wire: connected to the metal case. If a fault makes the live wire touch the case, the case would become live (230 V) and anyone touching it would get a shock. With the earth wire, the current flows through the low-resistance earth path instead — a large current, which melts the fuse and cuts the supply, and the case stays at 0 V. Appliances with plastic cases are double insulated and need no earth wire.

Why the switch and fuse are in the live wire (10.39): opening the switch (or melting the fuse) in the live wire disconnects the appliance from the 230 V, so nothing inside is live when it is off. In the neutral wire they would stop the current but leave the appliance connected to 230 V — still dangerous to touch.

Live to earth (10.41): there is a pd of 230 V between the live wire and the earth (the ground, water pipes, a person standing on the floor). Any connection between them — a bare live wire touched by a person — gives a large current through the connection: an electric shock, or a fire. That is also why water (a conductor) and mains electricity are kept apart.

The case therefore cannot stay at 230 V, so a user touching it does not get a shock.

sections.title: Key words: state what is meant by…

parts.title: The definitions
parts.html:
"State what is meant by" asks for the definition. Learn these as sentences.

TermWhat to write (mark-scheme form)Not this
Electric currentThe rate of flow of charge; in metals a flow of electrons. Unit ampere (A) = coulomb per second."the flow of electricity"
ChargeCarried by electrons (−) and protons (+); measured in coulombs (C); Q = I × t."the amount of current"
Potential differenceThe energy transferred per unit charge passing through a component; the volt is a joule per coulomb."the push" / "the amount of electricity"
ResistanceThe ratio of pd to current for a component, R = V ÷ I, in ohms (Ω); how hard it is to drive current through it."something that slows the current down"
Series circuitComponents connected one after another in a single loop: same current through each, pd shared."in a line"
Parallel circuitComponents connected in separate branches across the same two points: same pd across each, current shared."side by side"

LDRA light-dependent resistor: resistance decreases as the light intensity increases."a light sensor"
PowerThe energy transferred per second; watt (W) = joule per second. P = E ÷ t = I × V."how strong it is"
Direct currentMovement of charge in one direction only; supplied by cells and batteries."a constant current"
Alternating currentMovement of charge that changes direction repeatedly; UK mains 50 Hz, about 230 V."current that goes up and down"

sections.title: Core practical: I–V characteristics of a resistor and a filament lamp
equations: \text{vary } V \text{ with the variable resistor; read } I \text{ and } V;\ R = V/I

parts.title: The circuit and the method
parts.html:
1. Set up the circuit: supply, variable resistor, ammeter and the component (resistor first) in series; voltmeter across the component.
  2. Adjust the variable resistor to the lowest current; record the current (A) and the pd (V).
  3. Move the slider to increase the pd in steps (say 0.5 V), recording I and V each time, up to the component's rated pd.
  4. Reverse the connections to the supply (swap the leads) and repeat, to get the negative values.
  5. Switch off between readings (or take them quickly) so the component does not warm up and change its resistance; repeat each reading and take a mean.
  6. Replace the resistor with the filament lamp and repeat.
  7. Plot I (y) against V (x); the shape gives the resistance behaviour; $R = V/I$ at any point.

Control variables: the same component, the same temperature (as far as possible), the same meters. The June 2024 scheme (Q8(a)) gave one mark each for the variable resistor in series, the ammeter in series with the lamp and the voltmeter in parallel with the lamp; Q8(b)(i) credited data-logging for "collecting data in a short time" or "simultaneous current and voltage readings" — "more accurate" was ignored. The June 2022 report (Q2(c), the same circuit used on a length of resistance wire): "labelling and inserting the resistance wire carefully was the key to scoring maximum marks" — draw and label every component.

parts.title: The 6-mark method
parts.question: Describe how to investigate how the current in a filament lamp varies with the potential difference across it. (6 marks)
steps: Circuit: connect the lamp in series with an ammeter, a variable resistor and a d.c. supply; connect a voltmeter across the lamp.
Vary: use the variable resistor to change the pd across the lamp in equal steps from 0 up to its rated pd.
Measure: at each setting record the pd from the voltmeter and the current from the ammeter.
Reverse: swap the connections to the supply and repeat, so that negative pds and currents are recorded.
Reliability: repeat each reading and calculate a mean; switch off between readings so the lamp's temperature does not drift.
Analyse: plot current (y) against pd (x); a curve that flattens shows the resistance increasing; calculate $R = V/I$ at points to confirm.

sections.title: Testing series and parallel circuits (10.17b)

parts.title: The two test circuits
parts.html:
Series test: two resistors in one loop with the cell; an ammeter anywhere in the loop (move it round to show the current is the same everywhere); a voltmeter across each resistor and across the cell: the two pds add up to the cell's pd, the bigger resistor taking the bigger share. Add a third resistor and the current falls — resistances add.

Parallel test: the two resistors in separate branches; an ammeter in each branch and one by the cell: the branch currents add up to the cell current; a voltmeter across either branch reads the same as the cell. Add a branch and the cell current rises — total resistance falls.

The June 2025 report (Q10(c), 6 marks): Level 3 answers had "correct circuit diagrams for both arrangements, with ammeters and voltmeters placed correctly", included expected values, and explained "voltage sharing" in series, "the current being shared between branches" in parallel and "the same current throughout the series circuit". Level 2 had one circuit done properly; Level 1 "a misplaced voltmeter and no parallel circuit". The spec also asks you to explain the design of such circuits (10.16): every component you add is there to measure one quantity, and the meters must not change what they measure (voltmeter high resistance, ammeter low).

Lamps: two identical lamps in series each get half the pd and are dim; unscrew one and the other goes out. In parallel each gets the full pd and is bright; unscrew one and the other is unaffected. The June 2022 report (Q2(b)): to say which circuit's lamp is brighter you need both the pd argument (the pd across it is halved in series) and the power argument — most gave one "but rarely both".

parts.question: Describe how a student could test the rules for current and potential difference in series and parallel circuits using two resistors, a cell, ammeters and voltmeters. (6 marks)
steps: Series circuit: connect the two resistors and an ammeter in one loop with the cell; a voltmeter across each resistor and one across the cell.

Move the ammeter to different positions: the current is the same at every point. The voltmeter readings across the two resistors add up to the reading across the cell (e.g. 2 V + 4 V = 6 V): the pd is shared.
Parallel circuit: connect the two resistors in separate branches across the cell; an ammeter in each branch and one next to the cell; a voltmeter across each branch.
The branch currents add up to the cell current (e.g. 0.3 A + 0.6 A = 0.9 A): the current is shared. Each voltmeter reads the same as the cell (6 V): the pd is the same across every branch.
Resistance: in series the current is smaller than with one resistor (resistances add); in parallel the cell current is larger (total resistance is less than either).
Check with $V = IR$ for each resistor in each circuit; repeat readings to be sure.

sections.title: Explaining the I–V curves, and the gradient trap
equations: R = \dfrac{V}{I}\ \text{at the point — not the gradient}

parts.title: Three explanations
parts.html:
Fixed resistor (at constant temperature): the current is proportional to the pd — double the pd, double the current — so $V/I$ is the same at every point: constant resistance, a straight line through the origin, the same in both directions. (Ohm's law.)

Filament lamp: as the pd rises, the current rises and the filament gets hotter (electron–ion collisions, N9). Hotter means the ions vibrate more, so the electrons collide with them more often and it is harder for the current to get through: the resistance increases. Each extra volt gives less extra current, so the graph flattens. Say the chain: pd ↑ → current ↑ → temperature ↑ → ions vibrate more → more collisions → resistance ↑.

Diode: made so that current can pass in one direction only. Reverse-biased, its resistance is very high and the current is zero; forward-biased, once the pd passes about 0.7 V its resistance becomes low and the current rises steeply.

The gradient trap. On an I–V graph (I on the y-axis) the gradient is $I/V = 1/R$, not $R$ — and for a curve the gradient at a point is not even that. The resistance at a point is $R = V \div I$ using the coordinates of the point. The 2024 scheme accepted "the gradient decreases as pd increases, so resistance increases" as a comparison, but a numerical resistance must come from V/I. If the axes are the other way round (V against I), the gradient of a straight line is R.

parts.title: Explain the lamp
parts.question: Explain why the resistance of a filament lamp increases as the potential difference across it increases. (3 marks)
steps: A larger pd drives a larger current, and the current heats the filament (energy transferred by electrons colliding with the lattice ions).
At a higher temperature the ions vibrate more, so the electrons collide with them more frequently.
More collisions make it harder for charge to flow for a given pd: the resistance increases — so the I–V graph flattens.

sections.title: Circuit calculations the hard way
equations: \text{series: find } R_{\text{total}}, \text{ then } I, \text{ then each } V = IR
\text{parallel: same } V \text{ on each branch; } I = V/R \text{ per branch}

parts.title: The method
parts.html:
Series: (1) add the resistances; (2) $I = V_{\text{supply}} \div R_{\text{total}}$ — this current is the same through everything; (3) each component's pd is $V = I \times R$; (4) check the pds add up to the supply. The pd is shared in proportion to the resistances: 10 Ω and 30 Ω in series across 8 V take 2 V and 6 V. Removing a resistor from a series circuit lowers the total resistance, so the current rises and the pd across each remaining resistor rises.

Parallel: (1) the pd across every branch is the supply pd; (2) each branch current is $I = V \div R_{\text{branch}}$; (3) the supply current is the sum of the branch currents; (4) if asked, the total resistance is $R = V_{\text{supply}} \div I_{\text{supply}}$ — and it comes out smaller than the smallest branch. Removing a branch lowers the supply current and raises the total resistance (the June 2024 3-marker, N6).

Mixed circuits go beyond what Edexcel asks you to calculate, but one idea covers them: a parallel pair behaves like one resistor of the value found in step (4), which then sits in series with the rest.

Units: mA to A and kΩ to Ω before anything else; and give the pd across a component, not "the voltage of the resistor".

sections.title: Sensing circuits: how an LDR or thermistor switches something
equations: \text{series pair: the bigger resistance takes the bigger share of the pd}

parts.title: Exploring and using the variation
parts.html:
Exploring the variation (10.21): to measure how the resistance of an LDR changes with light, put the LDR in a circuit with an ammeter in series and a voltmeter across it, change the light level (a lamp at different distances, or layers of tracing paper), and calculate $R = V/I$ each time. For a thermistor, put it in a water bath with a thermometer and change the temperature; take the readings quickly at each temperature. The June 2022 report (Q8(c)): "very few" could improve the method of measuring the thermistor's temperature — keep the thermistor fully in the water, stir, read the temperature at the moment the meters are read, and let the bath settle at each temperature.

Using it — the pd-sharing argument. Two components in series share the supply pd in proportion to their resistances. With an LDR in series with a fixed resistor:

  • In the dark the LDR's resistance is high, so it takes most of the pd and the fixed resistor gets little.
  • In the light the LDR's resistance is low, so it takes little of the pd and the fixed resistor gets most.

So the pd across the fixed resistor is a signal that follows the light level; it can switch a lamp (via a transistor or relay — not on the spec) when it crosses a set value. Swap the components and the signal rises in the dark instead: a night light. The same circuit with a thermistor gives a pd that follows temperature: a thermostat switches a heater off when the pd across the resistor rises past a value; a fire alarm switches a bell on.

parts.title: Explain the night light
parts.question: A night light uses a sensing circuit: a fixed resistor in series with an LDR, with the lamp's control connected across the LDR. Explain why the lamp comes on when it gets dark. (3 marks)
steps: As it gets dark the resistance of the LDR increases.
The LDR and the fixed resistor are in series and share the supply pd in proportion to their resistances, so the LDR's share — the pd across the LDR — increases.
When the pd across the LDR rises above the switching value, the control switches the lamp on; in daylight the LDR's resistance and share of pd are low and the lamp stays off.

QuestionChain

parts.title: The 6-mark safety explanation
parts.question: A metal-cased kettle is connected to the mains with a three-core cable and a fused plug. Explain how the design keeps the user safe if the live wire inside the kettle comes loose and touches the case. (6 marks)
steps: The live wire is at 230 V; if it touches the metal case, the case would become live and a user touching it would get a shock.
The case is connected to the earth wire, which is at 0 V and provides a low-resistance path from the case to earth.
So a large current flows from the live wire, through the case and the earth wire, to earth.
The large current exceeds the rating of the fuse in the live wire, so the fuse wire heats up and melts…
…which breaks the circuit and disconnects the kettle from the live supply; the case cannot remain at 230 V.

The fuse is in the live wire so that, once it has melted, no part of the kettle is still connected to 230 V; the insulation on each wire and the cable clamp make the fault unlikely in the first place.

sections.title: Explaining with electrons: current, pd, resistance and heat
equations: \text{current: electrons drift},\ \text{pd: energy per coulomb},\ \text{resistance: collisions}

parts.title: The model in four sentences
parts.html:
• Current: free electrons drift through the metal when a pd is applied; the current is the charge passing per second. Electrons are not used up — the same number leave a lamp as enter it, which is why the current is the same all round a series circuit and why it is conserved at junctions.
  • Potential difference: the energy transferred per coulomb. The cell gives each coulomb a fixed amount of energy (its pd); each component takes some of it as the charge passes (the pd across it). The energy per coulomb given equals the energy per coulomb taken — so the pds across series components add up to the cell's pd. It is energy that is transferred, not voltage "used up" and not current "used up".
  • Resistance: electrons collide with the ions of the lattice; the more often, the harder it is to drive current for a given pd. Longer wire → more collisions → more resistance; thicker wire → more paths → less; hotter → ions vibrate more → more collisions → more.
  • Heating: each collision transfers energy from the electrons to the ions, which vibrate more: the resistor's temperature rises and the energy is dissipated to the surroundings as thermal energy. The June 2023 report (Q2(b)(iv)) praised "fewer electrons per second collide with the ions" as the reason a smaller current heats a wire less.

parts.title: Series pd in terms of energy
parts.question: A 6 V battery is connected to two lamps in series. The pd across one lamp is 2 V. Explain, in terms of energy, why the pd across the other is 4 V. (3 marks)
steps: The battery transfers 6 J to every coulomb of charge that passes through it (pd = energy per coulomb).
Each coulomb transfers 2 J in the first lamp (its pd is 2 V)…

…and the energy a coulomb carries round the circuit must all be transferred by the time it returns, so the other lamp transfers the remaining 4 J per coulomb: 4 V. (Energy is conserved; the pds add up.)

questions.text: A student says: "The current is used up by the first lamp, so the second lamp in series is dimmer." Explain what is wrong with this. (2)
questions.model:
• Current is a flow of electrons, which are not used up: the same number per second leave the lamp as enter it, so the current is the same in both lamps.
  • What the lamps take from the charge is energy (pd); two identical lamps in series are equally bright (and both dimmer than one alone, because each has half the pd).

questions.text: Explain, in terms of electrons, why a longer wire has a larger resistance. (2)
questions.model:
• Electrons moving through the wire collide with the ions of the lattice.
  • In a longer wire there are more collisions on the way through, so it is harder to drive a current for the same pd — larger resistance.

questions.text: The pd across a resistor is 3 V. This means…
options: each coulomb passing through it transfers 3 J
it has a resistance of 3 Ω
questions.explain: Volt = joule per coulomb.

questions.text: Explain why a smaller current makes a wire warm less. (2)
questions.model:
• A smaller current means fewer electrons per second pass through the wire…
  • …so there are fewer collisions with the ions per second, less energy is transferred to the ions' vibration, and the wire's temperature rises less.

questions.text: Why is the current the same at every point in a series circuit?
options: Because the voltage is the same everywhere
Because charge is conserved: electrons are not used up or stored, so the charge passing per second is the same at every point
questions.explain: Conservation of charge.

parts.title: The thermistor plan
parts.question: Plan an investigation to find how the resistance of a thermistor changes with temperature. (6 marks)
steps: Variables: change the temperature (independent), measure the resistance (dependent); use the same thermistor and supply throughout.
Circuit: thermistor in series with an ammeter and a low-voltage supply, voltmeter across the thermistor; resistance from $R = V/I$.

facts.q: Position, mass and charge of a proton, neutron and electron?
facts.a: Proton: nucleus, 1, +1. Neutron: nucleus, 1, 0. Electron: shells, very small, −1.

facts.q: What is electric current?
facts.a: The rate of flow of charge; in metals a flow of free electrons. 1 A = 1 C/s.

facts.q: Which way do electrons move, and which way is conventional current?
facts.a: Electrons: − to +. Conventional current: + to −.

facts.q: Why do metals conduct?
facts.a: They have free (delocalised) electrons that drift through the lattice when a pd is applied.

facts.q: Where does an ammeter go, and what does it measure?
facts.a: In series with the component; current, in amps.

facts.q: Where does a voltmeter go, and what does it measure?
facts.a: In parallel with (across) the component; potential difference, in volts.

facts.q: Which line of the cell symbol is positive?
facts.a: The long thin line.

facts.q: Why must a voltmeter never be in series?
facts.a: Its resistance is very high, so it would almost stop the current.

facts.q: How are a thermistor and an LDR drawn?
facts.a: Both a resistor rectangle: the thermistor with a bent line through it, the LDR with two arrows pointing in.

facts.q: Equation linking charge, current and time?
facts.a: Q = I × t (C = A × s). Convert mA to A and minutes to seconds first.

facts.q: What is needed for a current to flow?
facts.a: A closed (complete) circuit and a source of potential difference.

facts.q: What happens to current at a junction?
facts.a: It is conserved: total current in = total current out.

facts.q: What is potential difference?
facts.a: The energy transferred per unit charge (per coulomb) passing through a component. 1 V = 1 J/C.

facts.q: Equation linking energy, charge and pd?
facts.a: E = Q × V (J = C × V).

facts.q: What does the pd across a component tell you?
facts.a: How many joules each coulomb transfers in that component.

facts.q: Equation linking pd, current and resistance?
facts.a: V = I × R; R = V ÷ I in ohms (Ω).

facts.q: What happens to the current if the resistance in a circuit increases (same pd)?
facts.a: It decreases (I = V/R).

facts.q: How does a variable resistor change the current?
facts.a: Moving the slider changes the length of resistance wire in the circuit, changing the resistance and so the current.

facts.q: kΩ and mA — what do you do before substituting?
Series circuit: current, pd, resistance?
facts.a: Same current everywhere; pd shared (adds up to the supply, bigger R takes more); resistances add.

facts.q: Parallel circuit: current, pd, resistance?
facts.a: Current splits at junctions (branch currents add up); same pd across every branch; total resistance less than the smallest branch.

facts.q: Why does adding a resistor in series increase the total resistance?
facts.a: The current must pass through both, one after the other — more to push through, so less current for the same pd.

facts.q: Why does adding a resistor in parallel decrease the total resistance?
facts.a: It gives the current another path; the pd is unchanged but the total current increases, so R = V/I is smaller.

facts.q: Why are house lights wired in parallel?
facts.a: Each gets the full mains pd and can be switched independently; one failing leaves the rest on.

facts.q: I–V graph of a fixed resistor?
facts.a: A straight line through the origin: current proportional to pd, constant resistance.

facts.q: I–V graph of a filament lamp?
facts.a: A curve that flattens as pd increases (both directions): the resistance increases as the filament gets hotter.

facts.q: I–V graph of a diode?
facts.a: Zero current for reverse pd; for forward pd, nothing until about 0.7 V then a steep rise. Current in one direction only.

facts.q: How do you find the resistance at a point on an I–V graph?
facts.a: R = V ÷ I using the point's coordinates — not the gradient.

facts.q: How does an LDR's resistance depend on light?
facts.a: It decreases as the light intensity increases (high in the dark).

facts.q: How does a thermistor's resistance depend on temperature?
facts.a: It decreases as the temperature increases (NTC).

facts.q: Uses of an LDR and a thermistor?
facts.a: LDR: automatic lights at dusk, screen brightness. Thermistor: thermostats, fire alarms, engine temperature sensors.

facts.q: Thermistor vs variable resistor?
facts.a: Thermistor changes resistance by itself with temperature; a variable resistor is changed by hand.

facts.q: Why does a current heat a resistor?
facts.a: Electrons collide with the lattice ions, making them vibrate more — a higher temperature; the energy is dissipated to the surroundings.

facts.q: How do you reduce unwanted heating in wires?
facts.a: Use low-resistance wires: thick (large cross-section), short, good conductor (copper). Insulation does not reduce it.

facts.q: Devices that use the heating effect?
facts.a: Heaters, kettles, toasters, filament lamps, fuses.

facts.q: What is power, and its unit?
facts.a: Energy transferred per second; watts (1 W = 1 J/s). P = E ÷ t.

facts.q: The electrical power equations?
facts.a: P = I × V and P = I² × R.

facts.q: Energy transferred by a device?
facts.a: E = I × V × t, or E = P × t (t in seconds).

facts.q: Why is P = I × V?
facts.a: Each coulomb transfers V joules and I coulombs pass each second, so I × V joules per second.

facts.q: What does a power rating tell you?
facts.a: How fast the device transfers energy from the supply: energy = power × time.

facts.q: d.c. vs a.c.?
facts.a: d.c.: charge moves in one direction only (cells, batteries). a.c.: the movement of charge changes direction repeatedly (the mains).

facts.q: UK mains frequency and pd?
facts.a: 50 Hz, about 230 V, a.c.

facts.q: Live, neutral, earth: colours and pds?
facts.a: Live brown 230 V; neutral blue 0 V; earth green-and-yellow 0 V.

facts.q: What does the live wire do? The neutral?
facts.a: Live carries the current to the appliance at 230 V; neutral completes the circuit back to the supply at 0 V.

facts.q: What does a fuse do?
facts.a: Its thin wire melts when the current exceeds its rating, breaking the circuit. (It melts — it does not blow.)

facts.q: What does a circuit breaker do?
facts.a: An automatic switch that trips when the current is too large; faster than a fuse and can be reset.

facts.q: What does the earth wire do?
facts.a: Connects the metal case to earth; if the live touches the case, a large current flows through the low-resistance earth path and melts the fuse, so the case cannot stay live.

facts.q: Why are switches and fuses in the live wire?
facts.a: Breaking the live wire disconnects the appliance from 230 V; in the neutral the appliance would stay live.

facts.q: Why is a connection between live and earth dangerous?
facts.a: There is 230 V between them, so a large current flows through whatever makes the connection — a person gets a shock, a fault can start a fire.

facts.q: What is double insulation?
facts.a: A plastic (insulating) case that cannot become live, so no earth wire is needed.

facts.q: The I–V practical circuit?
facts.a: Supply, variable resistor and ammeter in series with the component; voltmeter across the component.

facts.q: How do you get negative values in the I–V practical?
facts.a: Reverse the connections to the supply and repeat.

facts.q: Why switch off between readings in the I–V practical?
facts.a: So the component does not warm up and change its resistance.

facts.q: What is the variable resistor for in the I–V practical?
facts.a: To change the pd across (and current in) the component for a range of readings.

facts.q: Series test: where do the meters go and what do they show?
facts.a: Ammeter anywhere in the loop (same current everywhere); voltmeter across each resistor — the pds add up to the cell's.

facts.q: Parallel test: where do the meters go and what do they show?
facts.a: Ammeter in each branch (currents add up to the cell current); voltmeter across a branch reads the cell pd.

facts.q: Two lamps in series, one removed?
facts.a: The other goes out: one path, the circuit is broken.

facts.q: Why is a lamp brighter in parallel than in series with another?
facts.a: It has the full pd across it (not a share), so a larger current and a larger power P = IV.

facts.q: Why does a lamp's resistance rise with pd?
facts.a: More current → hotter filament → ions vibrate more → electrons collide with them more often → higher resistance.

facts.q: Why is a resistor's I–V graph straight?
facts.a: At constant temperature the collisions do not change, so current is proportional to pd and R is constant.

facts.q: Is the gradient of an I–V graph the resistance?
facts.a: No. With I on the y-axis the gradient of a straight line is 1/R; for a curve use R = V/I at the point.

facts.q: Series method?
facts.a: Add the resistances → I = V/R → each pd = I × R → check they add up to the supply.

facts.q: Parallel method?
facts.a: Supply pd across each branch → I = V/R per branch → add for the supply current → total R = V/I (less than the smallest branch).

facts.q: Two resistors in series share the pd how?
facts.a: In proportion to their resistances: 10 Ω and 30 Ω across 8 V take 2 V and 6 V.

facts.q: LDR in series with a fixed resistor: what happens to the pds as it gets dark?
facts.a: The LDR's resistance rises, so it takes a bigger share of the pd; the pd across the fixed resistor falls.

facts.q: How does a thermistor thermostat work?
facts.a: Warmer → thermistor resistance falls → its share of pd falls, the fixed resistor's rises → past a set value the heater is switched off.

facts.q: How do you investigate a thermistor's resistance against temperature?
facts.a: Thermistor in a stirred water bath with a thermometer; ammeter in series, voltmeter across; R = V/I at each temperature.

facts.q: How do you choose a fuse for an appliance?
facts.a: I = P/V, then the lowest standard rating (3 A, 5 A, 13 A) above that current.

facts.q: Energy from a power rating?
facts.a: E = P × t with P in watts and t in seconds (kW × 1000; hours × 3600).

facts.q: The commonest error in E = IVt questions?
facts.a: Not converting kW/MJ and minutes/hours to W, J and seconds; and not stating the unit of a calculated time.

facts.q: The fuse chain?
facts.a: Current exceeds the rating → fuse wire heats and melts → circuit broken → appliance disconnected from the live supply.

facts.q: The earth-wire chain?
facts.a: Live touches the case → earth wire is a low-resistance path → large current to earth → fuse melts → circuit broken → case cannot stay live.

facts.q: Fuse vs circuit breaker?
facts.a: Both break the circuit when the current is too large; a breaker trips faster and can be reset, a fuse melts and must be replaced.

facts.q: Why is a 13 A fuse wrong for a 0.3 A lamp?
facts.a: A fault current of a few amps would not melt it, so the lamp could overheat without the supply being cut.

facts.q: Is current 'used up' by a lamp?
facts.a: No. Electrons are not used up; the current is the same before and after. What is transferred is energy (pd).

facts.q: Why do pds in series add up to the cell's pd?
facts.a: The cell gives each coulomb a fixed energy; the components take it in shares; energy is conserved, so the shares add to the total.

facts.q: Why does a longer wire have more resistance?
facts.a: More collisions between the electrons and the ions on the way through.

facts.q: Why does a smaller current heat a wire less?
facts.a: Fewer electrons per second → fewer collisions with the ions per second → less energy to the ions' vibration.

facts.q: Variables in the I–V investigation?
facts.a: Independent: pd; dependent: current; control: the component and its temperature.

facts.q: Variables in the thermistor investigation?
facts.a: Independent: temperature; dependent: resistance (from V/I); control: the thermistor and the supply pd.

facts.q: The accuracy detail for the thermistor investigation?
facts.a: Thermistor fully submerged beside the thermometer, water stirred, meters read at the moment the temperature is read.

facts.q: State what is meant by: electric current.
facts.a: The rate of flow of charge; in metals a flow of electrons. Unit ampere (A) = coulomb per second.

facts.q: State what is meant by: charge.
facts.a: Carried by electrons (−) and protons (+); measured in coulombs (C); Q = I × t.

facts.q: State what is meant by: potential difference.
facts.a: The energy transferred per unit charge passing through a component; the volt is a joule per coulomb.

facts.q: State what is meant by: resistance.
facts.a: The ratio of pd to current for a component, R = V ÷ I, in ohms (Ω); how hard it is to drive current through it.

facts.q: State what is meant by: series circuit.
facts.a: Components connected one after another in a single loop: same current through each, pd shared.

facts.q: State what is meant by: parallel circuit.
facts.a: Components connected in separate branches across the same two points: same pd across each, current shared.

facts.q: State what is meant by: ohmic conductor.
facts.a: A component whose current is proportional to the pd across it (constant resistance): a straight I–V line through the origin.

facts.q: State what is meant by: diode.
facts.a: A component that allows current in one direction only.

facts.q: State what is meant by: thermistor.
facts.a: A resistor whose resistance decreases as its temperature increases.

facts.q: State what is meant by: LDR.
facts.a: A light-dependent resistor: resistance decreases as the light intensity increases.

facts.q: State what is meant by: power.
facts.a: The energy transferred per second; watt (W) = joule per second. P = E ÷ t = I × V.

facts.q: State what is meant by: direct current.
facts.a: Movement of charge in one direction only; supplied by cells and batteries.

facts.q: State what is meant by: alternating current.
facts.a: Movement of charge that changes direction repeatedly; UK mains 50 Hz, about 230 V.

facts.q: State what is meant by: live wire.
facts.a: The brown wire at 230 V (alternating) that carries the current to the appliance; the switch and fuse are in it.

facts.q: State what is meant by: neutral wire.
facts.a: The blue wire at 0 V that completes the circuit back to the supply.

facts.q: State what is meant by: earth wire.
facts.a: The green-and-yellow wire at 0 V connected to the metal case; a low-resistance path for a fault current so the fuse melts.

facts.q: State what is meant by: fuse.
facts.a: A thin wire in the live wire that melts when the current exceeds its rating, breaking the circuit.

facts.q: State what is meant by: circuit breaker.
facts.a: An automatic switch that trips (opens) when the current is too large; can be reset.

types.name: Charge, current and time
types.method: Charge is current multiplied by time. Current must be in amps and time in seconds, so convert mA to A (divide by 1000) and minutes to seconds (multiply by 60) before you substitute. To find I or t, rearrange: I = Q / t and t = Q / I.
commonErrors: Leaving time in minutes, so the charge comes out 60 times too small
Forgetting to change mA into A before multiplying
Dividing the wrong way round when finding the time

steps: Known: I = 0.25 A, t = 2 minutes = 2 × 60 = 120 s. Unknown: Q.
Q = I × t
Q = 30 C

types.name: Potential difference, current and resistance
types.method: Potential difference is current multiplied by resistance. Put current in amps and resistance in ohms, so change mA to A (divide by 1000) and kΩ to Ω (multiply by 1000) first. To find I or R, rearrange: I = V / R and R = V / I.
commonErrors: Multiplying V by I to find R instead of dividing
Using a kΩ value as if it were in ohms
Giving the answer for a current in mA when the question asked for amps, or the other way round

types.name: Energy transferred by a charge
types.method: Energy transferred is charge multiplied by potential difference. Charge in coulombs and p.d. in volts gives energy in joules. If the question gives a current and a time instead of a charge, find Q = I × t first. To find Q or V, rearrange: Q = E / V and V = E / Q.
commonErrors: Multiplying current by potential difference and calling the result energy
Forgetting to convert kJ to J before rearranging
Using the time in minutes when finding the charge first

types.name: Electrical power
types.method: Electrical power is current multiplied by potential difference, or current squared multiplied by resistance. Choose the form that uses the two quantities you are given: I and V, or I and R. Change kW to W (multiply by 1000) before rearranging. To find I from P and V use I = P / V; to find R from P and I use R = P / I².
commonErrors: Forgetting to square the current in P = I² × R
Leaving the power in kW while the other quantities are in base units
Picking P = I × V when the question gives resistance and no p.d.

worked.question: A kettle connected to the 230 V mains takes a current of 10 A. Calculate the power of the kettle.
steps: Known: I = 10 A, V = 230 V. Unknown: P. We have I and V, so use P = I × V.

P = I² × R → R = P / I²

types.name: Energy, power and time
types.method: Energy transferred is power multiplied by time, and because power is I × V this is also current multiplied by p.d. multiplied by time. Time must be in seconds: multiply minutes by 60 and hours by 3600. Change kW to W and kJ to J before rearranging. To find P or t, rearrange: P = E / t and t = E / P.
commonErrors: Using the time in minutes or hours instead of seconds
Forgetting that a kW is 1000 W and a kJ is 1000 J
Multiplying current by time and forgetting the potential difference

types.name: Series and parallel circuits
types.method: In series the current is the same everywhere, the p.d.s across the components add up to the supply p.d., and the total resistance is the resistances added together. In parallel every branch has the same p.d. as the supply, and the branch currents add up to the current from the supply. Decide which rule applies, then use V = I × R on the part of the circuit you know about.
commonErrors: Adding resistances when the components are in parallel
Using the supply p.d. across one series component instead of the p.d. across that component
Forgetting that the current from the battery is the sum of the branch currents in parallel

types.name: Reading electrical graphs
types.method: On a current–potential difference graph, read the current and the p.d. at the marked point and divide: R = V / I. On a resistance–temperature graph for a thermistor you simply read the resistance off at the temperature asked.
